entries.7a5dd8cbe64810377d9aa18b6de9524ac7e05b8f: <div sID="gen19823" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Hos.8" sID="Hos.8"/> <div eID="gen19823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19824" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19825" type="x-p"/> This chapter, as that before, divides itself into the sins and punishments of Israel; every verse almost declares both, and all to bring them to repentance. When they saw the malignant nature of their sin, in the descriptions of that, they could not but be convinced now much it was their duty to repent of what was so bad in itself; and when they saw the mischievous consequences of their sin, in the predictions of them, they could not but see how much it was their interest to repent for the preventing of them. I. The sin of Israel is here set forth, 1. In many general expressions, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.12">12,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">14</reference>. 2. In many particular instances; setting up kings without God (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">ver. 4</reference>), setting up idols against God (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4-Hos.8.6">ver. 4-6, 11</reference>), and courting alliances with the neighbouring nations,, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8-Hos.8.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. 3. In this aggravation of it, that they still kept up a profession of religion and relation to God, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">14</reference>. II. The punishment of Israel is here set forth as answering to the sin. God would bring an enemy upon them, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">3</reference>. All their projects should be blasted, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">ver. 7</reference>. Their confidence both in their idols and in their foreign alliances should disappoint them, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">ver. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.10">10</reference>. Their strength at home should fail them, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">ver. 14</reference>. Their sacrifices should have no reckoning made of them, and their sins should have a reckoning made for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">ver. 13</reference>.
entries.e9a111a86f14bb5595d26fd32ddc3a9a75b238c0: <div eID="gen19825" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19824" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Sin and Punishment of Israel; Crimes Charged against Israel; Sottish Idolatry of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  745.)</title> <div sID="gen19826" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="italic">Set</hi> the trumpet to thy mouth. <hi type="italic">He shall come</hi> as an eagle against the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because they have transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law. <hi type="super">2</hi> Israel shall cry unto me, My God, we know thee. <hi type="super">3</hi> Israel hath cast off <hi type="italic">the thing that is</hi> good: the enemy shall pursue him. <hi type="super">4</hi> They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes, and I knew <hi type="italic">it</hi> not: of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast <hi type="italic">thee</hi> off; mine anger is kindled against them: how long <hi type="italic">will it be</hi> ere they attain to innocency? <hi type="super">6</hi> For from Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> it also: the workman made it; therefore it <hi type="italic">is</hi> not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces. <hi type="super">7</hi> For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up. <div eID="gen19826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19827" type="x-p"/> The reproofs and threatenings here are introduced with an order to the prophet to <hi type="italic">set the trumpet to his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">v. 1</reference>), thus to call a solemn assembly, that all might take notice of what he had to deliver and take warning by it. He must sound an alarm, must, in God's name, proclaim war with this rebellious nation. An enemy is coming with speed and fury to seize their land, and he must awaken them to expect it. Thus the prophet must do the part of a watchman, that was by sound of trumpet to call the besieged to stand to their arms, when he saw the besiegers making their attack, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.3">Ezek. xxxiii. 3</reference>. The prophet must <hi type="italic">lift up his voice like a trumpet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.1">Isa. lviii. 1</reference>), and the people must hearken to the sound of the trumpet, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer. vi. 17</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen19827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19828" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a general charge drawn up against them as sinners, as rebels and traitors against their sovereign Lord. 1. They have <hi type="italic">transgressed my covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">v. 1</reference>. They have not only transgressed the command (every sin does that), but they have <hi type="italic">transgressed the covenant;</hi> they have been guilty of such sins as break the original contract; they have revolted from their allegiance, and violated the marriage-covenant by their spiritual whoredom; they have, in effect, declared that they will be no longer God's people, nor take him for their God; that is <hi type="italic">transgressing the covenant.</hi> They have not only done foolishly, but have dealt deceitfully. 2. They have <hi type="italic">trespassed against my law</hi> in many particular instances. God's law is the rule by which we are to walk; and this is the malignity of sin, that it trespasses upon the bounds set us by that law. 3. They have <hi type="italic">cast off the thing that is good.</hi> They have <hi type="italic">put away</hi> and <hi type="italic">rejected good,</hi> that is, God himself; so some understand it, and very fitly. He is good, and does good, and is our goodness. <hi type="italic">There is none good but one, that is God,</hi> the fountain of all good. They have <hi type="italic">cast him off,</hi> as not desiring to have any thing more to do with him. God was abandoning them to ruin, and here gives the reason for it. Note, God never casts off any till they first cast him off. Or, as we read it, They have cast off <hi type="italic">the thing that is good;</hi> they have cast off the service and worship of God, which is, in effect, <hi type="italic">casting God off.</hi> They have cast off that which denominates men good; they have cast off the fear of God, and the regard of man, and all sense of virtue and honesty. Observe, <hi type="italic">They have transgressed my covenant;</hi> it has come to this at last; for <hi type="italic">they trespassed against my law.</hi> Breaking the command made way for breaking the covenant; and they did that, for they <hi type="italic">cast off that which was good;</hi> there it began first. They <hi type="italic">left off to be wise and to do good,</hi> and then they went all to naught, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.3">Ps. xxxvi. 3</reference>. See the method of apostasy; men first cast off that which is good; then those omissions make way for commissions; and frequent actual transgressions of God's law bring men at length to an habitual renunciation of his covenant. When men cast off praying, and hearing, and sabbath-sanctification, and other things that are good, they are in the high road to a total forsaking of God. <div eID="gen19828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19829" type="x-p"/> II. Here are general threatenings of wrath and ruin for their sin: <hi type="italic">The enemy shall come as an eagle against the house of the Lord,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">v. 3</reference>) <hi type="italic">shall pursue him.</hi> If by <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord</hi> we understand the temple at Jerusalem, by the eagle that comes against it we must suppose to be meant either Sennacherib, who had taken all the fenced cities of Judah, laid siege to Jerusalem (and, no doubt, aimed at the house of the Lord, to lay that waste, as he had done the temples of the gods of other nations), or Nebuchadnezzar, who burnt the temple and made a prey of the vessels of the temple. But, if we make it to point at the destruction of the kingdom of the ten tribes by the king of Assyria, we must reckon it is the body of that people which as Israelites, to whom <hi type="italic">pertained the adoption, the glory, and the covenants,</hi> is here called the <hi type="italic">house of the Lord.</hi> They thought their being so would be their protection; but the prophet is directed to tell them that now they had lost the life and spirit of their religion, though they still retained the name and form of it, they were but as a carcase to which the eagles and other birds of prey should be gathered together. The enemy shall pursue them <hi type="italic">as an eagle,</hi> so swiftly, so strongly, so furiously. Note, Those who break their covenant of friendship with God expose themselves to the enmity of all about them, to whom they make themselves a cheap and easy prey; and their having been <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord,</hi> and his living temples, will be no excuse nor refuge to them. See <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen19829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19830" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the people's hypocritical claim of relation to God, when they were in trouble and distress (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Israel shall cry unto me;</hi> when either they are threatened with these judgments, and would plead an exemption, or when the judgments are inflicted on them and they apply to God for relief, <hi type="italic">pouring out a prayer when God's chastening is upon them,</hi> they will plead that among them <hi type="italic">God is known</hi> and his <hi type="italic">name is great</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.1">Ps. lxxvi. 1</reference>) and in their distress will pretend to that knowledge of God's ways which in their prosperity they <hi type="italic">desired not,</hi> but <hi type="italic">despised.</hi> They will then cry unto God, will call him their God, and (as impudent beggars) will tell him they are well acquainted with him, and have known him long. Note, There are many who in works deny God, and disown him, yet, to serve a turn, will profess that they <hi type="italic">know him,</hi> that they know more of him than some of their neighbours do. But what stead will it stand a man in to be able to say, <hi type="italic">My God, I know thee,</hi> when he cannot say, "My God, I love thee," and "My God, I serve thee, and cleave to thee only?" <div eID="gen19830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19831" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the prophet's expostulation with them, in God's name (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">How long will it be ere they attain to innocency?</hi> It is not meant of absolute innocency (that is what the guilty can never attain to); but how long will it be ere they repent and reform, ere they become innocent in this matter, and free from the sin of idolatry? They are wedded to their idols; how long will it be ere they are weaned from them, ere <hi type="italic">they are able to get clear of them?</hi> so it might be rendered. This intimates that custom in sin makes it very difficult for men to part with it. It is hard to cleanse from that filthiness, either of flesh or spirit, which has been long wallowed in. But God speaks as if he thought the time long till sinners cast away their iniquities and come to live a new life. He complains of their obstinacy; it is that which keeps his anger against them burning, which would soon be turned away if they did but <hi type="italic">attain to innocency</hi> from those sins that kindled it. They in trouble cry, <hi type="italic">How long</hi> will it be ere God return to us in a way of mercy? but they do not hear him ask, <hi type="italic">How long</hi> will it be ere they return to God in a way of duty? <div eID="gen19831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19832" type="x-p"/> V. Here are some particular sins which they are charged with, are convicted of the folly of, and warned of the fatal consequences of, and for which God's <hi type="italic">anger is kindled against them.</hi> <div eID="gen19832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19833" type="x-p"/> 1. In their civil affairs. They set <hi type="italic">up kings without God,</hi> and in contempt of him, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">v. 4</reference>. So they did when they rejected Samuel, in whom the Lord was their king, and chose Saul, that they might be <hi type="italic">like the nations.</hi> So they did when they revolted from their allegiance to the house of David, and set up Jeroboam, wherein, though they fulfilled God's secret counsel, yet they aimed not at his glory, nor consulted his oracle, nor applied to him by prayer for direction, nor had any regard to his providence, but were led by their own humour and hurried on by the impetus of their own passions. So they did now about the time when Hosea prophesied, when it seems to have grown fashionable to <hi type="italic">set up kings,</hi> and depose them again, according as the contenders for the crown could make an interest, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.8">2 Kings xv. 8</reference>, &c. Note, We cannot expect comfort and success in our affairs when we go about them, and go on in them, without consulting God and acknowledge not him in all our ways: "They <hi type="italic">set up kings,</hi> and <hi type="italic">I knew it not,</hi> that is, I did not know it from them, they did not ask <hi type="italic">counsel at my mouth,</hi> whether they might lawfully do it or whether it would be best for them to do it, though they had prophets and oracles with whom they might have advised." They <hi type="italic">looked not to the Holy One of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Isa. xxxi. 1</reference>. Nor did the princes do as Jephthah, who, before he took upon him the government, <hi type="italic">uttered all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.11.11">Judg. xi. 11</reference>. Note, Those that are entrusted with public concerns, and particularly with the election and nomination of magistrates, ought to take God along with them therein, by desiring his direction and designing his honour. <div eID="gen19833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19834" type="x-p"/> 2. In their religious matters they did much worse; for they <hi type="italic">set up calves against God,</hi> in competition with him and contradiction to him. "Of <hi type="italic">their silver and their gold</hi> which God <hi type="italic">gave them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">multiplied</hi> to them, that they might serve and honour him with them, they have <hi type="italic">made them idols.</hi>" They called them <hi type="italic">gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.28">1 Kings xii. 28</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold thy gods, O Israel!</hi>) but God calls them <hi type="italic">idols;</hi> the word signifies <hi type="italic">griefs,</hi> or <hi type="italic">troubles,</hi> because they are offensive to God and will be ruining to those that worship them. <hi type="italic">Their silver and their gold they have made to them idols;</hi> so the words are, referring primarily to the images of their gods, which they made of gold and silver, especially the golden calves at Dan and Bethel. Idolaters spare no cost in worshipping their idols. But they are very applicable to the spiritual idolatry of the covetous: <hi type="italic">Their silver and their gold</hi> are the gods they place their happiness in, set their hearts upon, to which they pay their homage, and in which they put their confidence. Now, to show them the folly of their idolatry, he tells them, <div eID="gen19834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19835" type="x-p"/> (1.) Whence their gods came. Trace them to their original, and they will be found the creatures of their own fancies and the work of their own hands, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">v. 6</reference>. The calf they worshipped is here called <hi type="italic">the calf of Samaria,</hi> because it is probable that when Samaria, in Ahab's time, became the metropolis of the kingdom, a calf was set up there to be near the court, besides those at Dan and Bethel, or perhaps one of those was removed thither; for those that are for new gods will still be for newer. Now let them consider what this god of theirs owed its rise and being to. [1.] To their own invention and institution: <hi type="italic">From Israel was it also,</hi> not from the God of Israel (he expressly forbade it), but from Israel; it was a device of their own (some think), not borrowed from any of their neighbours, no, not from the Egyptians, for, though they worshipped Apis in a living cow, they never worshipped a <hi type="italic">golden calf;</hi> that was from Israel; it was <hi type="italic">their own iniquity.</hi> Now could that be worthy of their worship which was a contrivance of their own? It was <hi type="italic">from Israel,</hi> that is, the gold and silver of which it was made were collected from the people of Israel by a brief: it was a poor god that was framed by contribution. [2.] It was owing to the skill and labour of the craftsman, <reference osisRef="Deut.27.15">Deut. xxvii. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">The workmen made it, therefore it is not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">v. 6</reference>. This is a very cogent conclusive argument, and the inference so very plain that one would think their own thoughts should have suggested it to them, so as to make them ashamed of their idolatry. What can be more absurd than for men to worship that as a god, giving being and good to them, which they themselves gave being to (both matter and form), but could not give life to? A made god is no God. This is a self-evident truth; and yet St. Paul was accused as a criminal for preaching that <hi type="italic">those are no gods which are made with hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.19.26">Acts xix. 26</reference>. And, here, this which should have turned them from their idols comes in as a reason why they were inseparably wedded to them; therefore they could not attain to innocency because it was <hi type="italic">from themselves;</hi> they were willing to have gods of their own to do what they pleased with, that they themselves might do what they pleased. <div eID="gen19835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19836" type="x-p"/> (2.) What their gods would come to. If they are not gods, they will not last; nay, if they pretend to be gods, they will be reckoned with: <hi type="italic">The calf of Samaria shall be broken to pieces,</hi> and those that would not yield to the force of the former argument shall be convinced by this that it is not God, but an <hi type="italic">unprofitable idol,</hi> as the Chaldee calls it. It shall be <hi type="italic">broken to shivers,</hi> like a potter's vessel, though it be a golden calf. It shall be <hi type="italic">chips</hi> or <hi type="italic">saw-dust;</hi> it shall be a <hi type="italic">spider's web;</hi> so St. Jerome. It seems to allude to Moses's grinding to powder the golden calf that was in his time. This shall be served as that was. Sennacherib boasted what he had done to <hi type="italic">Samaria and her idols,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.11">Isa. x. 11</reference>. Note, Deifying any creature makes way for the destruction of it. If they had made vessels and ornaments for themselves of their silver and gold, they might have remained; but, if they make gods of them, they shall be <hi type="italic">broken to pieces.</hi> <div eID="gen19836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19837" type="x-p"/> (3.) What their gods would bring them to. The breaking of them to pieces would be a disappointment to those who trusted in them. But that was not all: <hi type="italic">They have</hi> made to themselves idols, <hi type="italic">that they may be cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">v. 4</reference>), that their gold and silver, which they so abused, may be cut off (so some take it), nay, that they may themselves be cut off from God, from their own land, from the land of the living. Their idolatry will as certainly end in their extirpation as if they had purposely designed it. And, when this proves to be the effect of their sin, what relief will they have from the gods wherein they trusted? None at all: "<hi type="italic">Thy calf, O Samaria! has cast thee off;</hi> it cannot give thee any help in thy distress, and the pleasure thou now takest in it will vanish, and be no pleasure to thee." Those that were justly sent to the gods whom they had chosen found them <hi type="italic">miserable comforters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 14</reference>. If men will not quit the love and service of sin, yet they shall certainly lose all the delights and profits of it. If Samaria had continued firm and faithful to the God of Israel, he would have been a present powerful help to her; but the calf she preferred before him was a broken reed. The case will be the same with those that make their silver and their gold their god. It will <hi type="italic">cast them off,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">profit them in the day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.12">Ezek. vii. 12</reference>. Note, Those that suffer themselves to be deceived into any idolatries will certainly find themselves deceived in them. Cardinal Wolsey owned that if he had served his God as faithfully as he had served his prince he would not have <hi type="italic">cast him off,</hi> as his prince did, in his old age. Their disappointment in their idols is illustrated (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">v. 7</reference>) by a similitude which intimates both that and the destruction which God brought upon them for their idolatry. [1.] They got no good to themselves by worshipping idols: <hi type="italic">They have sown the wind.</hi> They have put themselves to a great deal of trouble and expense to make and worship their idols, have made a business of it as much as the husbandman does of sowing his corn, in expectation of reaping some mighty advantage from it, and that they should be as prosperous and victorious as the neighbouring nations were, that worshipped idols. But it is all a cheat; it is like <hi type="italic">sowing the wind,</hi> which can yield no increase; they <hi type="italic">labour in vain, labour for the wind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Eccl. v. 16</reference>. They take great pains to no purpose, and <hi type="italic">weary themselves for very vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Hab. ii. 13</reference>. Those that make an idol of this world do so; they <hi type="italic">set their eyes on that which is not,</hi> which, like the wind, makes a great noise, but has nothing substantial in it. [2.] They brought ruin upon themselves by it: They shall <hi type="italic">reap the whirlwind,</hi> a <hi type="italic">great whirlwind</hi> (so the word signifies), which shall hurry them away and dash them to pieces. They not only have not their false gods for them but they set the true God against them; their favour will stand them in no more stead than the wind, but his wrath will do them more mischief than a whirlwind. As a man sows, so shall he reap. "If it may be supposed that a man should sow the wind, and cover it with earth, or keep it there for a while penned up, what could he expect but that it should be forced by its being shut up, and the accession of what might increase its strength, to break forth again in greater quantities with greater violence?" So Dr. Pocock. They promise themselves plenty, peace, and victory, by worshipping idols, but their expectations come to nothing. What they sow never comes up; it has <hi type="italic">no stalk,</hi> no blade, or, if it have, <hi type="italic">the bud shall yield no meal;</hi> it shall be as the thin ears in Pharaoh's dream, that were blasted with the <hi type="italic">east wind,</hi> and there was nothing in them. Or <hi type="italic">if it yield,</hi> if they do prosper for a while in their idolatrous courses, <hi type="italic">the strangers shall swallow it up;</hi> it shall be so far from doing them any service that it shall be but as a bait to invite strangers to invade them, and as a spoil to enrich those strangers and enable them to do so much the more mischief. Note, The service of idols is an unprofitable service, and the works of darkness are unfruitful; nay, in the end they will be pernicious. <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Rom. vi. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">The end of those things is death.</hi> Those that <hi type="italic">sow iniquity</hi> reap <hi type="italic">vanity:</hi> nay, those that <hi type="italic">sow to the flesh, reap corruption.</hi> The hopes of sinners will be cheats, and their gains will be snares.
entries.614e9b0cd222963d147ca264966c30fb93403630: <div eID="gen19837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of Israel; The Crimes of the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 745.)</title> <div sID="gen19838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Israel is swallowed up: now shall they be among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein <hi type="italic">is</hi> no pleasure. <hi type="super">9</hi> For they are gone up to Assyria, a wild ass alone by himself: Ephraim hath hired lovers. <hi type="super">10</hi> Yea, though they have hired among the nations, now will I gather them, and they shall sorrow a little for the burden of the king of princes. <hi type="super">11</hi> Because Ephraim hath made many altars to sin, altars shall be unto him to sin. <hi type="super">12</hi> I have written to him the great things of my law, <hi type="italic">but</hi> they were counted as a strange thing. <hi type="super">13</hi> They sacrifice flesh <hi type="italic">for</hi> the sacrifices of mine offerings, and eat <hi type="italic">it; but</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> accepteth them not; now will he remember their iniquity, and visit their sins: they shall return to Egypt. <hi type="super">14</hi> For Israel hath forgotten his Maker, and buildeth temples; and Judah hath multiplied fenced cities: but I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour the palaces thereof. <div eID="gen19838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19839" type="x-p"/> It was the honour and happiness of Israel that they had but one God to trust to and he all-sufficient in every strait, and but one God to serve, and he well worthy of all their devotions. But it was their sin, and folly, and shame, that they knew not when they were well off, that they forsook their own mercies for lying vanities; for, <div eID="gen19839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19840" type="x-p"/> I. They multiplied their alliances (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have hired lovers,</hi> or (as the margin reads it) <hi type="italic">they have hired loves.</hi> They were at great expense to purchase the friendship of the nations about them, that otherwise had no value nor affection at all for them, nor cared for having any thing to do with them but only upon the Shechemites' principles—<hi type="italic">Shall not their cattle and their substance be ours?</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.34.23">Gen. xxxiv. 23</reference>. Had Israel maintained the honour of their peculiarity, the surrounding nations would have continued to admire them <hi type="italic">as a wise and understanding people;</hi> but, when they profaned their own crown, their neighbours despised them, and they had no interest in them further than they paid dearly for it. But those surely have behaved ill among their neighbours who have no loves, no lovers, but what they hire. See here, 1. The contempt that Israel lay under among the nations (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Israel is swallowed up,</hi> devoured by strangers, their land eaten up (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">v. 7</reference>), and themselves too, and, being impoverished, they have quite lost their credit and reputation, like a merchant that has become a bankrupt, so that they are <hi type="italic">among the Gentiles as a vessel wherein is no pleasure,</hi> a vessel of <hi type="italic">dishonour</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">2 Tim. ii. 20</reference>), a <hi type="italic">despised broken vessel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jer. xxii. 28</reference>. None of their neighbours have any value for them, nor care to have any thing to do with them. Note, Those that have professed religion, if they degenerate and grow profane, are of all men the most contemptible. <hi type="italic">If the salt have lost its savour,</hi> it is fit for nothing but to be <hi type="italic">trodden under foot of men.</hi> Or it denotes their dispersion and captivity <hi type="italic">among the Gentiles;</hi> they shall be among them poor and prisoners; and who has pleasure in such? 2. The court that Israel made to the nations notwithstanding (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">v. 9</reference>): They have <hi type="italic">gone to Assyria,</hi> to engage the king of Assyria to help them; and herein they are as a <hi type="italic">wild ass alone by himself,</hi> foolish, headstrong, and unruly; they will have their way, and nothing shall <hi type="italic">hold them in,</hi> no, not the bridle of God's laws, nothing shall <hi type="italic">turn them back,</hi> no, not the sword of God's wrath. They take a course by themselves, and the effect will be that, like a <hi type="italic">wild ass by himself,</hi> they will be the easier and surer prey to the lion. See <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job xi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jer. ii. 24</reference>. Note, Man is in nothing more like the wild ass's colt than in seeking for that succour and that satisfaction in the creature which are to be had in God only. 3. The crosses that they were likely to meet with in their alliances with the neighbouring nations (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though they have hired among the nations,</hi> and hoped thereby to prevent their own ruin, yet <hi type="italic">now will I gather them,</hi> as <hi type="italic">the sheaves in the floor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 12</reference>); so that what they provided for their own safety shall but make them the easier prey to their enemies. Note, There is no fence against the judgments of God, when they come with commission; nay, that which men hire for their own preservation often contributes to their own destruction. See <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Isa. vii. 20</reference>. The king of Assyria, whose friendship they courted, called himself a <hi type="italic">king of princes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Isa. x. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Are not my princes altogether kings?</hi> He laid <hi type="italic">burdens</hi> upon Israel, levied taxes upon them, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19-2Kgs.15.20">2 Kings xv. 19, 20</reference>. And for these <hi type="italic">they shall sorrow a little;</hi> this shall be but a little burden to them in comparison of what they may further expect; or they will be but little sensible of this grievance, will not lay it to heart, and therefore may expect heavier judgments. <hi type="italic">They have begun to be diminished</hi> (so some read it), <hi type="italic">by the burden of the king of princes;</hi> but this is only the <hi type="italic">beginning of sorrows</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.8">Matt. xxiv. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">the beginning of revenges,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.42">Deut. xxxii. 42</reference>. Note, God often comes gradually with his judgments upon a provoking people, that he may show how slow he is to wrath, and may awaken them to repentance; but those that are made to <hi type="italic">sorrow a little,</hi> if they are not thereby brought to sorrow after a godly sort, will, another day, be made to sorrow a great deal, to sorrow everlastingly. <div eID="gen19840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19841" type="x-p"/> II. They multiplied their altars and temples. Observe, <div eID="gen19841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19842" type="x-p"/> 1. How they denied <hi type="italic">the power of godliness,</hi> and wholly cast that off (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have written to him the great things of my law;</hi> this intimates the privilege they enjoyed, as having God's statutes and judgments made known to them, and being entrusted with the lively oracles. Note, (1.) The things of God's law are <hi type="italic">magnalia Dei—the great things of God.</hi> They are things that proclaim the greatness of the Law-maker, and things of great use and great importance to us; they are our life, and our eternal welfare depends upon our observance of them and obedience to them; they will make us great if we make a right use of them; and they are things which God will magnify and make honourable. (2.) It is a great privilege to have the things of God's law written; thus they are reduced to a greater certainty, spread the further, and last the longer, with much less danger of being embezzled and corrupted than if they were transmitted by word of mouth only. (3.) The things of God's law are of his own writing; for Moses and the prophets were his amanuenses, and holy men wrote as they were moved by the Holy Ghost. (4.) It is the advantage of those that are members of the visible church that these great things are written <hi type="italic">to them,</hi> are intended for their direction, and so they must receive them; what things were written in former ages <hi type="italic">were written for our learning,</hi> and are profitable for us. And, if those were happy who had the <hi type="italic">great things of God's law</hi> written to them, how much happier are we who have the gospel written to us! But see how this privilege was slighted; these great things of the law were <hi type="italic">counted as a strange thing,</hi> as unintelligible and unreasonable (which might <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> be slighted, because not to be fathomed, not to be accounted for), or as foreign, and things of no concernment to them, things that they had nothing to do with nor were to be governed by; they used those things as strangers, which they were shy of, and knew not how to bid welcome. <hi type="italic">We desire not the knowledge of thy ways.</hi> Note, [1.] God having written to us the great things of his law, we ought to make them familiar to us, as our nearest relations (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.3-Prov.7.4">Prov. vii. 3, 4</reference>); for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> we have them written, that they may <hi type="italic">talk with us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Prov. vi. 22</reference>. [2.] We make nothing of the things of God's law if we make strange of them, as if they did not affect us and therefore we need not be affected with them. <div eID="gen19842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19843" type="x-p"/> 2. How they kept up the form of godliness notwithstanding, and to what little purpose they did so. <div eID="gen19843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19844" type="x-p"/> (1.) They multiplied their altars (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ephraim made many altars to sin.</hi> God appointed that there should be but one altar for sacrifice (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.3">Deut. xii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.12.5">5</reference>); but the ten tribes, having forsaken that, would still be thought very devout, and zealous for the honour of God, and, as if they would make amends for the affront they put on God's altar, they made <hi type="italic">many altars,</hi> dedicated to the God of Israel, whom hereby they intended, or at least pretended, to give glory to; but that would not justify their violation of God's express command, nor would the example of the patriarchs, who before the law of Moses had many altars. No, they <hi type="italic">made many altars to sin</hi> (that is, they did that which turned into sin to them), and therefore these <hi type="italic">altars shall be unto</hi> them <hi type="italic">to sin,</hi> that is, God will charge it upon them as a heinous sin, and put that upon the score of their crimes which they designed to be for the expiation of their crimes. Or they shall be to them an occasion of further sin. Their multiplying of altars dedicated to the God of Israel would introduce altars dedicated to other gods. Note, It is a great sin to corrupt the worship of God, and it will be charged as sin upon those that do it, how plausible soever their pretensions may be. And the way of this, as other sins, is down-hill; those that once deviate from the fixed rule of God's commands will wander endlessly. <div eID="gen19844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19845" type="x-p"/> (2.) They multiplied their sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">v. 13</reference>. Their altars were smoking altars: They <hi type="italic">sacrificed flesh for the sacrifices of God's offerings,</hi> and they celebrated their feasts upon their sacrifices; they were at a great expense upon their devotions, and (as those commonly are who set up their own inventions in the room of divine institutions) were very zealous in their way; as if they hoped by their impositions on themselves to atone for the contempt of the great atonement, and by their observing a ceremonial law of their own to excuse themselves from the obligation of all God's moral precepts. But how did they speed? [1.] God makes no reckoning of their services: <hi type="italic">The Lord accepts them not.</hi> How should he, when they did not offer their sacrifice upon that altar which alone <hi type="italic">sanctified the gift,</hi> and when they only sacrificed flesh, but not the spiritual sacrifice of a penitent believing heart? Note, Those services only are acceptable to God which are performed according to the rule of his word, and <hi type="italic">through Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>. [2.] He takes that occasion to reckon with them for their sins; now will he, instead of pardoning their iniquity and blotting out their sins, as they expected, <hi type="italic">remember their iniquity</hi> and <hi type="italic">visit their sins.</hi> Such an <hi type="italic">abomination to the Lord</hi> are the <hi type="italic">sacrifices of the wicked</hi> that they provoke him to call them to an account for all their other abominations. When they think by their sacrifices to bribe the Judge of heaven and earth into a connivance at their wickedness he will resent that as the highest affront they can put upon him, and it shall be the measure-filling sin. Note, A petition for leave to sin amounts to an imprecation of the curse for sin, and so it shall be answered, <hi type="italic">according to the multitude of the idols.</hi> "I will punish their sins, <hi type="italic">for they shall return to Egypt;</hi>" they shall be carried captive into Assyria, which shall be to them a house of bondage, as Egypt was to their fathers. Or it refers to <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">Deut. xxviii. 68</reference>, where returning to Egypt is made to close and complete the miseries of that sinful nation. <div eID="gen19845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19846" type="x-p"/> (3.) They multiplied their temples, and these also in honour of the true God, as they pretended, but really in contempt of the choice he had made of Jerusalem to <hi type="italic">put his name there. Israel has forgotten his Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">v. 14</reference>. They pretended to know him, and yet forgot him, for they <hi type="italic">liked not to retain God in their knowledge,</hi> when the remembrance of him would give check to their lusts. It was an aggravation of their sin in forgetting God that he was <hi type="italic">their Maker</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15 Deut.32.18">Deut. xxxii. 15, 18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job xxxv. 10</reference>), as nothing obliges us more to remember him than that he is <hi type="italic">our Creator,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1">Eccl. xii. 1</reference>. "He has <hi type="italic">forgotten his Maker, and builds temples;</hi> he seems by the temples he builds to me mindful of his Maker, and to be desirous still to keep him in mind, and yet really he has forgotten him, because he has cast off the fear of him." Some by temples here understand <hi type="italic">palaces,</hi> for so the word sometimes signifies. "<hi type="italic">He has forgotten his Maker,</hi> and yet is so secure and haughty that he sets his judgments at defiance, as Nebuchadnezzar did when he said, <hi type="italic">Is not this great Babylon that I have built?</hi>" Judah is likewise charged with <hi type="italic">multiplying fenced cities,</hi> and trusting in them for safety, when the judgments of God were abroad. To fortify their cities in subjection and subordination to God was well enough; but to fortify them in opposition to God, and without any regard to him or his providence (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa. xxii. 11</reference>), shows their hearts to be desperately <hi type="italic">hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.</hi> But <hi type="italic">none ever hardened his heart against God and prospered,</hi> nor shall they. <hi type="italic">God will send a fire upon his cities,</hi> upon the cities both of Judah and Israel, not only the head-cities of Jerusalem and Samaria, but all the other cities of those two kingdoms, and it shall devour not only the cottages, but <hi type="italic">the palaces thereof;</hi> though ever so strong, the fire shall master them; though ever so stately and sumptuous, the fire shall not spare them. This was fulfilled when all the cities of Israel were laid in ashes by the king of Assyria, and all the cities of Judah by the king of Babylon. The fires they both kindled were of his sending; and when he judges he will overcome.  <chapter eID="Hos.8"/> <div eID="gen19846" type="x-p"/>

entries.f358ca88349a2b9fe267d307d21aeda0b1834022: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12338"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.8.1-Hos.8.14">Ho 8:1-14</reference>. Prophecy of the Irruption of the Assyrians, in Punishment for Israel's Apostasy, Idolatry, and Setting Up of Kings without God's Sanction.</title> <div sID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">Ho 8:14</reference>, Judah is said to multiply fenced cities; and in <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7-Hos.8.9">Ho 8:7-9</reference>, Israel, to its great hurt, is said to have gone up to Assyria for help. This answers best to the reign of Menahem. For it was then that Uzziah of Judah, his contemporary, built fenced cities (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.10">9, 10</reference>). Then also Israel turned to Assyria and had to pay for their sinful folly a thousand talents of silver (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>) [Maurer].<div eID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12338"/><hi type="bold">1. Set the trumpet, &c.--</hi>to give warning of the approach of the enemy: "To thy palate (that is, 'mouth,' <reference osisRef="Job.31.30">Job 31:30</reference>, Margin) the trumpet"; the abruptness of expression indicates the suddenness of the attack. So <reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">Ho 5:8</reference>.<div eID="gen22538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... eagle--</hi>the Assyrian (<reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">De 28:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Ha 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against ... house of ... Lord--</hi>not the temple, but Israel viewed as the family of God (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.15">Ho 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.7">Nu 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.8">Zec 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.3.2">He 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1Pe 4:17</reference>). <div eID="gen22540" type="x-p"/>
entries.45508b9cbec126633bdc915dba165d6a8d59ffd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12339"/><div sID="gen22541" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12339"/><hi type="bold">2. My God, we know thee--</hi>the singular, "My," is used distributively, each one so addressing God. They, in their hour of need, plead their knowledge of God as the covenant-people, while in their acts they acknowledge Him not (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.7.21">Mt 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.16">Tit 1:16</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Is 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.4">Jr 7:4</reference>). The Hebrew joins "Israel," not as English Version, with "shall cry," but "We, Israel, know thee"; God denies the claim thus urged on the ground of their descent from Israel. <div eID="gen22541" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef6c8df486d2cf4e562a02ea52567e9615f98559: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12340"/><div sID="gen22542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12340"/><hi type="bold">3. Israel--</hi>God repeats the name in opposition to their use of it (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">Ho 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the thing that is good--</hi>Jerome translates, "God" who is good and doing good (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.68">Psa 119:68</reference>). He is the chief object rejected, but with Him also all that is good.<div eID="gen22543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the enemy shall pursue him--</hi>in just retribution from God. <div eID="gen22544" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5a942d6cd443afd75782b2bca51c57da1fc8a07: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12341"/><div sID="gen22545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12341"/><hi type="bold">4. kings ... not by me--</hi>not with My sanction (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.31">1Ki 11:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.20">12:20</reference>). Israel set up Jeroboam and his successors, whereas God had appointed the house of David as the rightful kings of the whole nation.<div eID="gen22545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I knew it not--</hi>I approved it not (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen22546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of ... gold ... idols--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Ho 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may be cut off--</hi>that is, though warned of the consequences of idolatry, as it were with open eyes they rushed on their own destruction. So <reference osisRef="Jer.27.10">Jr 27:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.8">44:8</reference>. <div eID="gen22548" type="x-p"/>
entries.da554af97dddce0aa6b842c312e6ede9412f1601: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12342"/><div sID="gen22549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12342"/><hi type="bold">5. hath cast thee off--</hi>As the ellipsis of thee is unusual, Maurer translates, "thy calf is abominable." But the antithesis to <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">Ho 8:3</reference> establishes English Version, "Israel hath cast off the thing that is good"; therefore, in just retribution, "thy calf hath cast thee off," that is, is made by God the cause of thy being cast off (<reference osisRef="Hos.10.15">Ho 10:15</reference>). Jeroboam, during his sojourn in Egypt, saw Apis worshipped at Memphis, and Mnevis at Heliopolis, in the form of an ox; this, and the temple cherubim, suggested the idea of the calves set up at Dan and Beth-el.<div eID="gen22549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how long ... ere they attain to innocency?--</hi>How long will they be incapable of bearing innocency? [Maurer]. <div eID="gen22550" type="x-p"/>
entries.9643f55887a1073e4719b182a71c744dca58c372: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12343"/><div sID="gen22551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12343"/><hi type="bold">6. from Israel was it--</hi>that is, the calf originated with them, not from Me. "It also," as well as their "kings set up" by them, "but not by Me" (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Ho 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen22551" type="x-p"/>
entries.db9effa66238ec431f5ba33f2dfdd426110476a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12344"/><div sID="gen22552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12344"/><hi type="bold">7. sown ... reap--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pr 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>). "Sow ... wind," that is, to make the vain show of worship, while faith and obedience are wanting [Calvin]. Rather, to offer senseless supplications to the calves for good harvests (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Ho 2:8</reference>); the result being that God will make them "reap no stalk," that is, "standing corn." Also, the phraseology proverbially means that all their undertakings shall be profitless (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.29">Pr 11:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Ec 5:16</reference>).<div eID="gen22552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bud--</hi>or, "growth."<div eID="gen22553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>foreigners (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Ho 7:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22554" type="x-p"/>
entries.e35ecba6d578ecfbe967a7099a9c17610a62eac0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12345"/><div sID="gen22555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12345"/><hi type="bold">8. vessel wherein is no pleasure--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.41.12">Psa 41:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jr 22:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.38">48:38</reference>). <div eID="gen22555" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5039fb2a2efae02628ab6dfa4073924a37ef82d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12346"/><div sID="gen22556" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12346"/><hi type="bold">9. gone ... to Assyria--</hi>referring to Menahem's application for Pul's aid in establishing him on the throne (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">7:11</reference>). Menahem's name is read in the inscriptions in the southwest palace of Nimrod, as a tributary to the Assyrian king in his eighth year. The dynasty of Pul, or Phalluka, was supplanted at Nineveh by that of Tiglath-pileser, about 768 (or 760) B.C. Semiramis seems to have been Pul's wife, and to have withdrawn to Babylon in 768; and her son, Nabonassar, succeeding after a period of confusion, originated "the era of Nabonassar," 747 B.C. [G. V. Smith]. Usually foreigners coming to Israel's land were said to "go up"; here it is the reverse, to intimate Israel's sunken state, and Assyria's superiority.<div eID="gen22556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild ass--</hi>a figure of Israel's headstrong perversity in following her own bent (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.24">Jr 2:24</reference>).<div eID="gen22557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alone by himself--</hi>characteristic of Israel in all ages: "lo, the people shall dwell alone" (<reference osisRef="Num.23.9">Nu 23:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.8">Job 39:5-8</reference>).<div eID="gen22558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hired lovers--</hi>reversing the ordinary way, namely, that lovers should hire her (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.33">Eze 16:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.34">34</reference>). <div eID="gen22559" type="x-p"/>
entries.277c2e60dc14f19e2288f49daa83c2a89010877b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12347"/><div sID="gen22560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12347"/><hi type="bold">10. will I gather them--</hi>namely, the nations (Assyria, &c.) against Israel, instead of their assisting her as she had wished (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.37">Eze 16:37</reference>).<div eID="gen22560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22561" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a little--</hi>rather, "in a little" [Henderson]. English Version gives good sense: They shall sorrow "a little" at the imposition of the tribute; God suspended yet the great judgment, namely, their deportation by Assyria.<div eID="gen22561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the burden of the king of princes--</hi>the tribute imposed on Israel (under Menahem) by the Assyrian king Pul, (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19-2Kgs.15.22">2Ki 15:19-22</reference>), who had many "princes" under his sway (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Is 10:8</reference>). <div eID="gen22562" type="x-p"/>
entries.979810f981079c0fc7cb401926399311ad6d4ad2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12348"/><div sID="gen22563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12348"/>11. God in righteous retribution gives them up to their own way; the sin becomes its own punishment (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pr 1:31</reference>).<div eID="gen22563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many altars--</hi>in opposition to God's law (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.5">De 12:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.13">6, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen22564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to sin ... to sin--</hi>Their altars which were "sin" (whatever religious intentions they might plead) should be treated as such, and be the source of their punishment (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.30">1Ki 12:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.34">13:34</reference>). <div eID="gen22565" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f17caeb29c216bc8d9d9da0342a84a4141e0880: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12349"/><div sID="gen22566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12349"/><hi type="bold">12. great things of ... law--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">De 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.19.8">Psa 19:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.18">119:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.72">72</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.19">147:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">20</reference>). Maurer not so well translates, "the many things of My law."<div eID="gen22566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my law--</hi>as opposed to their inventions. This reference of Hosea to the Pentateuch alone is against the theory that some earlier written prophecies have not come down to us.<div eID="gen22567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strange thing--</hi>as if a thing with which they had nothing to do. <div eID="gen22568" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0241b53c5f0c81b8beb8358e11fe7f8b8149e37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12350"/><div sID="gen22569" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12350"/><hi type="bold">13. sacrifices of mine offerings--</hi>that is, which they offer to Me.<div eID="gen22569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eat it--</hi>Their own carnal gratification is the object which they seek, not My honor.<div eID="gen22570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22571" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>that is, "speedily."<div eID="gen22571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall return to Egypt--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Ho 9:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">11:11</reference>). The same threat as in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.68">De 28:68</reference>. They fled thither to escape from the Assyrians (compare as to Judah, Jr 42:1-44:30), when these latter had overthrown their nation. But see on <reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Ho 9:3</reference>. <div eID="gen22572" type="x-p"/>
entries.30eaff14dcf8b8930d1825d60a0e3884a00c226c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12351"/><div sID="gen22573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12351"/><hi type="bold">14. forgotten ... Maker--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">De 32:18</reference>).<div eID="gen22573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temples--</hi>to idols.<div eID="gen22574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22575" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Judah ... fenced cities--</hi>Judah, though less idolatrous than Israel, betrayed lack of faith in Jehovah by trusting more to its fenced cities than to Him; instead of making peace with God, Judah multiplied human defenses (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.8">Is 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.17">Jr 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.10">Mi 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen22575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will send ... fire upon ... cities--</hi>Sennacherib burned all Judah's fenced cities except Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.13">2Ki 18:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">palaces thereof--</hi>namely, of the land. Compare as to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.27">Jr 17:27</reference>. <chapter eID="Hos.8"/>

entries.ce760514cd015b04c6e5bde4d870162f1009ae93: <div eID="gen33744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33745" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with threatening some hostile invasion in short and broken sentences, full of rapidity, and expressive of sudden danger and alarm: "The trumpet to thy mouth; he cometh as an eagle," <reference osisRef="Hos.8.1">Hos 8:1</reference>. And why? For their hypocrisy, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.2">Hos 8:2</reference>; iniquity, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.3">Hos 8:3</reference>; treason (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.13">2Kgs 15:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.17">2Kgs 15:17</reference>) and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Hos 8:4</reference>; particularly the worshipping of the calves of Dan and Bethel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.5">Hos 8:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.6">Hos 8:6</reference>. The folly and unprofitableness of pursuing evil courses is then set forth in brief but very emphatic terms. The labor of the wicked is vain, like sowing of the wind; and the fruit of it destructive as the whirlwind. Like corn blighted in the bud, their toil shall have no recompense; or if it should have a little, their enemies shell devour it, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Hos 8:7</reference>. They themselves, too, shall suffer the same fate, and shall be treated by the nations of Assyria and Egypt as the vile sherds of a broken vessel, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.8">Hos 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">Hos 8:9</reference>. Their incorrigible idolatry is again declared to be the cause of their approaching captivity under the king of Assyria. And as they delighted in idolatrous altars, there they shall have these in abundance, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.10-Hos.8.14">Hos 8:10-14</reference>. The last words contain a prediction of the destruction of the fenced cities of Judah, because the people trusted in these for deliverance, and not in the Lord their God. <div eID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33749" type="x-p"/> Set the trumpet to thy mouth - Sound another alarm. Let them know that an enemy is fast approaching. <div eID="gen33749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> As an eagle against the house of the Lord - of this be a prophecy against Judah, as some have supposed, then by the eagle Nebuchadnezzar is meant, who is often compared to this king of birds. See <reference osisRef="Eze.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">Dan 7:4</reference>. <div eID="gen33750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33751" type="x-p"/> But if the prophecy be against Israel, which is the most likely, then Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, is intended, who, for his rapidity, avarice, rapacity, and strength, is fitly compared to this royal bird. He is represented here as hovering over the house of God, as the eagle does over the prey which he has just espied, and on which he is immediately to pounce.
entries.9c9bf442ccece05b3acbafe27982ecec4caa40e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33752" type="x-p"/> Israel shalt cry - The rapidity of the eagle's flight is well imitated in the rapidity of the sentences in this place. <div eID="gen33752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33753" type="x-p"/> My God, we know thee - The same sentiment, from the same sort of persons, under the same feelings, as that in the Gospel of St. Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.29">Mat 7:29</reference> : "Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? Then will I profess unto them, I never Knew You."
entries.83781613155a702943b4ac4ef6771635a15acb72: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33754" type="x-p"/> They have set up kings, but not by me - Properly speaking, not one of the kings of Israel, from the defection of the ten tribes from the house of David, was the anointed or the Lord. <div eID="gen33754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33755" type="x-p"/> I knew it not - It had not my approbation. In this sense the word know is frequently understood. <div eID="gen33755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33756" type="x-p"/> That they may be cut off - That is, They shall be cut off in consequence of their idolatry.
entries.779993bc0b9286c083ee063550e22e1e69f73b1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33757" type="x-p"/> Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off - Bishop Newcome translates: "Remove far from thee thy calf, O Samaria!" Abandon thy idolatry; for my anger is kindled against thee. <div eID="gen33757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33758" type="x-p"/> How long will it be ere they attain to innocency? - How long will ye continue your guilty practices? When shall it be said that ye are from these vices? The calf or ox, which was the object of the idolatrous worship of the Israelites, was a supreme deity in Egypt; and it was there they learned this idolatry. A white ox was worshipped under the name of Apis, at Memphis; and another ox under the name of Mnevis, was worshipped at On, or Heliopolis. To Osiris the males of this genus were consecrated, and the females to Isis. It is a most ancient superstition, and still prevails in the East. The cow is a most sacred animal among the Hindoos.
entries.2cd44b198885bf870a8d2e1d8a03a86a99110647: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33759" type="x-p"/> The workman made it; therefore it is not God - As God signifies the supreme eternal Good, the Creator and Upholder of all things, therefore the workman cannot make Him who made all things. This is an overwhelming argument against all idols. Nothing need be added. The workman has made them; therefore they are not God.
entries.4b1c0c4a311c58939c37ce6b263b4fcaa5534adf: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33760" type="x-p"/> They have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind - As the husbandman reaps the same kind of grain which he has sown, but in far greater abundance, thirty, sixty, or one hundred fold; so he who sows the wind shall have a whirlwind to reap. The vental seed shall be multiplied into a tempest so they who sow the seed of unrighteousness shall reap a harvest of judgment. This is a fine, bold, and energetic metaphor. <div eID="gen33760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33761" type="x-p"/> It hath no stalk - Nothing that can yield a blossom. If it have a blossom that blossom shall not yield fruit; if there be fruit, the sower shall not enjoy it, for strangers shall eat it. The meaning is, the labors of this people shall be utterly unprofitable and vain.
entries.df72cd9a4f267ab8a94e172052fb5db6e9464462: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33762" type="x-p"/> Now shall they be among the Gentiles - They shall be carried into captivity, and there be as a vessel wherein there is no pleasure; one soiled, unclean, infectious, to be despised, abhorred, not used. The allusion is to a rotten, corrupted skin-bottle; a bottle made of goat, deer, or calf hide, still commonly used in Asia and Africa. Some of them are splendidly ornamented. This is the case with one now before me made of a goat's skin well dressed, variously painted, and ornamented with leather fringes, tassels, etc. In such a bottle there might be pleasure; but the Israelites are compared to such a bottle, rough, ill-dressed, not ornamented, old, musty, and putrid. This shows the force of the comparison.
entries.f566b714da09d356972099b136a0443a5d7a0f57: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33763" type="x-p"/> They are gone up to Assyria - For succor. <div eID="gen33763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33764" type="x-p"/> A wild ass alone by himself - Like that animal, jealous of its liberty, and suffering no rival. If we may credit Pliny and others, one male wild ass will keep a whole flock of females to himself, suffer no other to approach them, and even bite off the genitals of the colts, lest in process of time they should become his rivals. "Mares singuli faeminarum gregibus imperitant; timent libidinis aemulos, et ideo gravidas custodiunt, morsuque natos mares castrant." - Hist. Nat., lib. viii., c. 30. The Israelites, with all this selfishness and love of liberty, took no step that did not necessarily lead to their thraldom and destruction. <div eID="gen33764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33765" type="x-p"/> Ephraim hath hired lovers - Hath subsidized the neighboring heathen states.
entries.36ee00a3bb72b7a879290b4450c093d7b9a40f0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33766" type="x-p"/> For the burden of the king of princes - The exactions of the Assyrian king, and the princes of the provinces.
entries.d0807d77287f612ebfd5bacc82819eba5c0ec4f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33767" type="x-p"/> Many altars to sin - Though it does not appear that the Jews in Babylon were obliged to worship the idols of the country, except in the case mentioned by Daniel, yet it was far otherwise with the Israelites in Assyria, and the other countries of their dispersion. Because they had made many altars to sin while they were in their own land, they were obliged to continue in the land of their captivity a similar system of idolatry against their will. Thus they felt and saw the evil of their idolatry, without power to help themselves.
entries.aaba857930aaffc2f53059a6a21a59a47bda2ff0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33768" type="x-p"/> I have written to him the great things of my law - I have as it were inscribed my laws to them, and they have treated them as matters in which they had no interest.
entries.a4b14c9ec3a46361e6386b8cf9770e97719daa94: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33769" type="x-p"/> They sacrifice flesh - Bp. Newcome translates thus: "They sacrifice gifts appointed unto me, and eat flesh." They offer to their idols the things which belong to Jehovah; or, while pretending to offer unto the Lord, they eat and drink idolatrously; and therefore the Lord will not accept them. <div eID="gen33769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33770" type="x-p"/> They shall return to Egypt - Many of them did return to Egypt after the conquest of Palestine by Shalmaneser, and many after the ruin of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar; but they had in effect returned to Egypt by setting up the worship of the golden calves, which were in imitation of the Egyptian Apis.
entries.294d6c8324fe5b3b9c441dc375915ec555a49fe9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33771" type="x-p"/> Israel hath forgotten his Maker - And therefore built temples to other gods. Judah had lost all confidence in the Divine protection, and therefore built many fenced cities. But the fire of God's anger burnt up both the temples and the fortified cities.  <chapter eID="Hos.8"/> <div eID="gen33771" type="x-p"/>

entries.a666c6326c2a0e5bd8ab363d0256e24129279581: <div eID="gen16231" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Judgment Consequent Upon Apostasy - Hosea 8-9:9</title> <div sID="gen16232" type="x-p"/> The coming judgment, viz., the destruction of the kingdom of the ten tribes, is predicted in three strophes, containing a fresh enumeration of the sins of Israel (1-7), a reference to the fall of the kingdom, which is already about to commence (Hos 8:8-14), and a warning against false security (Hos 9:1-9). <div eID="gen16232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16233" type="x-p"/> Hos 8:1-2 <div eID="gen16233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16234" type="x-p"/> The prophecy rises with a vigorous swing, as in Hos 5:8, to the prediction of judgment. Hos 5:1. <hi type="italic">“The trumpet to thy mouth! Like an eagle upon the house of Jehovah! Because they transgressed my covenant, and trespassed against my law.</hi> Hos 5:2. <hi type="italic">To me will they cry: My God, we know Thee, we Israel!” </hi> The first sentence of Hos 5:1 is an exclamation, and therefore has no verb. The summons issues from Jehovah, as the suffixes in the last sentences show, and is addressed to the prophet, who is to blow the trumpet, as the herald of Jehovah, and give the people tidings of the approaching judgment (see at Hos 5:8). The second sentence gives the alarming message to be delivered: like an eagle comes the foe, or the judgment upon the house of Jehovah. The simile of the eagle, that shoots down upon its prey with the rapidity of lightning, points back to the threat of Moses in Deu 28:49. The <hi type="italic">“house of Jehovah”</hi> is neither the temple at Jerusalem (Jerome, Theod., Cyr.), the introduction of which here would be at variance with the context; nor the principal temple of Samaria, with the fall of which the whole kingdom would be ruined (Ewald, Sim.), since the temples erected for the calf-worship at Daniel and Bethel are called <hi type="italic">Bēth bâmōth</hi>, not <hi type="italic">Bēth Yehōvâh</hi>; nor even the land of Jehovah, either here or at Hos 9:15 (Hitzig), for a land is not a house; but Israel was the house of Jehovah, as being a portion of the congregation of the Lord, as in Hos 9:15; Num 12:7; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jer 12:7</reference>; Zec 9:8; cf. οἶκος Θεοῦ in <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">Heb 3:6</reference> and 1Ti 3:15. The occasion of the judgment was the transgression of the covenant and law of the Lord, which is more particularly described in 1Ti 3:4. In this distress they will call for help to Jehovah: “My God (i.e., each individual will utter this cry), we know Thee?” <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> is in apposition to the subject implied in the verb. They know Jehovah, so far as He has revealed Himself to the whole nation of Israel; and the name Israel is in itself a proof that they belong to the people of God.
entries.0c8bd4d7783dfd21798a9ef98c647adfabca0909: Hos 8:3 <div eID="gen16234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16235" type="x-p"/> But this knowledge of God, regarded simply as a historical acquaintance with Him, cannot possibly bring salvation. Hos 8:3. <hi type="italic">“Israel dislikes good; let the enemy pursue it.”</hi> This is the answer that God will give to those who cry to Him. טוב denotes neither “Jehovah as the highest good” (Jerome) or as “the good One” (Sims.), nor “the good law of God” (Schmieder), but the good or salvation which Jehovah has guaranteed to the nation through His covenant of grace, and which He bestowed upon those who kept His covenant. Because Israel has despised this good, let the enemy pursue it.
entries.4694955d56ee93c342fc7fa320afd450d955889b: Hos 8:4 <div eID="gen16235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16236" type="x-p"/> The proof of Israel’s renunciation of its God is to be found in the facts mentioned in Hos 8:4. <hi type="italic">“They have set up kings, but not from me, have set up princes, and I know it not: their silver and their gold they have made into idols, that it may be cut off.” </hi> The setting up of kings and princes, not from Jehovah, and without His knowledge, i.e., without His having been asked, refers chiefly to the founding of the kingdom by Jeroboam I. It is not to be restricted to this, however, but includes at the same time the obstinate persistence of Israel in this ungodly attitude on all future occasions, when there was either a change or usurpation of the government. And the fact that not only did the prophet Ahijah foretel to Jeroboam I that he would rule over the ten tribes (1Ki 11:30.), but Jehu was anointed king over Israel by Elisha’s command (2 Kings 9), and therefore both of them received the kingdom by the express will of Jehovah, is not at variance with this, so as to require the solution that we have a different view here from that which prevails in the books of Kings, - namely, one which sprang out of the repeated changes of government and anarchies in this kingdom (Simson). For neither the divine promise of the throne, nor the anointing performed by the command of God, warranted their forcibly seizing upon the government, - a crime of which both Jeroboam and Jehu rendered themselves guilty. The way in which both of them paved the way to the throne was not in accordance with the will of God, but was most ungodly (see at 1Ki 11:40). Jeroboam was already planning a revolt against Solomon (1Ki 11:27), and led the gathering of the ten tribes when they fell away from the house of David 91 Kings Hos 12:2.). Of Jehu, again, it is expressly stated in 2Ki 9:14, that he conspired against Joram. And the other usurpers, just like the two already named, opened the way to the throne by means of conspiracies, whilst the people not only rebelled against the rightful heir to the throne at Solomon’s death, from pure dislike to the royal house of David, which had been appointed by God, and made Jeroboam king, but expressed their approval of all subsequent conspiracies as soon as they have been successful. This did not come from Jehovah, but was a rebellion against Him - a transgression of His covenant. To this must be added the further sin, viz., the setting up of the idolatrous calf-worship on the part of Jeroboam, to which all the kings of Israel adhered. It was in connection with this, that the application of the silver and gold to idols, by which Israel completely renounced the law of Jehovah, had taken place. It is true that silver was not used in the construction of the golden calves; but it was employed in the maintenance of their worship. למען יכּרת: that it (the gold and silver) may be destroyed, as more fully stated in Hos 8:6. למען describes the consequence of this conduct, which, though not designed, was nevertheless inevitable, as if it had been distinctly intended.
entries.c63c9645f44526ac4a8f32f04c750fe4b09a4cd6: Hos 8:5-6 <hi type="italic">“Thy calf disgusts, O Samaria; my wrath is kindled against them: how long are they incapable of purity.</hi> Hos 8:6. <hi type="italic">For this also is from Israel: a workman made it, and it is not God; but the calf of Samaria will become splinters.” Zânach</hi> (disgusts) points back to Hos 8:3. As Israel felt disgust at what was good, so did Jehovah at the golden calf of Samaria. It is true that <hi type="italic">zânach</hi> is used here intransitively in the sense of smelling badly, or being loathsome; but this does not alter the meaning, which is obvious enough from the context, namely, that it is Jehovah whom the calf disgusts. The calf of Samaria is not a golden calf set up in the city of Samaria; as there is no allusion in history to any such calf as this. Samaria is simply mentioned in the place of the kingdom, and the calf is the one that was set up at Bethel, the most celebrated place of worship in the kingdom, which is also the only one mentioned in Hos 10:5, Hos 10:15. On account of this calf the wrath of Jehovah is kindled against the Israelites, who worship this calf, and cannot desist. This is the thought of the question expressing disgust at these abominations. How long are they incapable of נקּין, i.e., purity of walk before the Lord, instead of the abominations of idolatry (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jer 19:4</reference>); not “freedom from punishment,” as Hitzig supposes. To לע יוּכלוּ, “they are unable,” we may easily supply “to bear,” as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.14">Isa 1:14</reference> and Psa 101:5. “For” (<hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>, Hos 8:6) follows as an explanation of the main clause in Hos 8:5, “Thy calf disgusts.” The calf of Samaria is an abomination to the Lord, for it is also out of Israel (Israel’s God out of Israel itself!); a workman made it, - what folly! והוּא is a predicate, brought out with greater emphasis by ו, <hi type="italic">et quidem</hi>, in the sense of iste. Therefore will it be destroyed like the golden calf at Sinai, which was burnt and ground to powder (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.20">Exo 32:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.21">Deu 9:21</reference>). The ἅπ. λεγ. שׁבבים, from Arab. <hi type="italic">sabb</hi>, to cut, signifies ruins or splinters.
entries.efdccd39c1882b251b3d10a2f1a89f08814b22f3: Hos 8:7 <div eID="gen16236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16237" type="x-p"/> This will Israel reap from its ungodly conduct. Hos 8:7. <hi type="italic">“For they sow wind, and reap tempest: it has no stalks; shoot brings no fruit; and even if it brought it, foreigners would devour it.” </hi> With this figure, which is so frequently and so variously used (cf. Hos 10:13; Hos 12:2; <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.8">Pro 22:8</reference>), the threat is accounted for by a general thought taken from life. The harvest answers to the sowing (cf. <reference osisRef="Gal.6.7-Gal.6.8">Gal 6:7-8</reference>). Out of the wind comes tempest. <hi type="italic">Wind</hi> is a figurative representation of human exertions; the <hi type="italic">tempest</hi>, of destruction.
